title: Will Republican gerrymanders become dummymanders?
contentHtml:
Last summer, Republicans triggered an unprecedentedly broad wave of mid-decade redistricting by drawing themselves a more favorable map in Texas. Gavin Newsom and Democrats countered in California. But Republicans, with an assist from GOP-friendly courts, seemingly emerged with the upper hand by the end of the process.

Excluding new boundaries that courts eventually rejected in Virginia and Missouri, seven states drew maps that were supposed to favor Republicans: Texas, Florida, Ohio, North Carolina, Louisiana, Tennessee and Alabama. Only two states got bluer: California and Utah, where a court required the creation of a Salt Lake City district after a judge ruled that a 4-0 Republican map had violated the state’s ban on partisan gerrymandering.

But if you look at the polls, Democrats are having something of a moment, redistricting be damned. Their lead on the generic congressional ballot is up to 8.6 points — or 9.3 with FLIPR’s likely voter adjustment. And they’re doing surprisingly well in polls of traditionally red states such as Texas, Kansas, and Alaska.

These facts aren’t inherently in tension with one another. Districting governs what we nerds call the “votes-to-seats” curve: not how many votes you win, but whether they translate into enough seats to win majorities and legislate effectively.

Plus, gerrymanders are usually designed to maximize a party’s upside in competitive elections, not necessarily to withstand waves. In the House, Democrats’ chances are up to 93 percent in FLIPR. It would take a massive October surprise or a bigger-than-2016 polling error to save the Republican majority there, despite Republicans’ aggressive redistricting. Instead, as the polls have gotten bluer, more and more red-leaning seats have come into play. Just last week, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee added six more House districts to its “Red to Blue” list.

Still, FLIPR’s mean projection for Democratic gains is “just” 23 seats. So rather than obsessing over dream or nightmare scenarios for either party, let’s focus today on what happens if the polls are basically right. (Wouldn’t that be nice for us election forecasters.) Democrats make big gains, but mostly concentrated in red states, and particularly among groups that most shifted Republican during the Trump Era, namely Hispanics and white working-class voters. Would they be big enough to make the new Republican maps backfire?
